patient_information: A 40-year-old male farmer from the Peruvian Amazon, who was found to be HTLV-1-positive 10 years prior to presentation. A recent HIV ELISA test was negative.
chief_complaint: A 4-month history of chronic productive cough and chest pain.
history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 4-month history of chronic productive cough, chest pain, dyspnoea on exertion, and a weight loss of about 20 kg. He denied diarrhoea, fever, or night sweats. Three and a half months earlier, he was hospitalized for similar complaints and presumptively diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis based on clinical and radiographic findings, despite three negative sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). He received first-line TB therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) but showed no clinical improvement, with persistence of his productive cough, which later included streaking of blood in the sputum. This led to his referral with a suspected diagnosis of multi-drug resistant TB.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a farmer from a rural area in the central Peruvian Amazon. He denies any recent travel.
vitals: Temperature was 37.2°C (98.96°F), blood pressure was 120/75 mmHg, pulse was 70 bpm regular, and respiratory rate was 15 breaths per minute.
physical_exam: The patient appeared fatigued and cachectic. On inspection, a few small, mobile, soft, and non-tender cervical and retroauricular lymph nodes were palpable. Examination of the lungs revealed crackles and rhonchi bilaterally. There was no hepatosplenomegaly, and the rest of the physical examination was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results showed a platelet count of 1093 x 10^9/L, indicating thrombocytosis; the rest of the full blood count was within normal limits. Three initial sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were negative, as were two subsequent AFB smears. The tuberculin skin test was also negative. A chest x-ray showed bilateral confluent reticulonodular infiltrates and multiple cavities in the right lung. A definitive diagnosis was made when a sputum KOH preparation revealed the characteristic yeast forms of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, which was subsequently grown in culture.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential diagnoses considered were multi-drug resistant TB (MDR TB), histoplasmosis, and paracoccidioidomycosis. While TB is endemic in Peru, MDR TB was considered less likely given the patient's origin from a rural area. Histoplasmosis was also less likely as its chronic form is more common in individuals with pre-existing lung disease. Paracoccidioidomycosis was deemed the most probable diagnosis given the patient's age, gender, occupation, origin, and clinical presentation. Less common possibilities included paragonimiasis or pulmonary hydatid cyst.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was initially treated with a full course of first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy for several months without any clinical improvement. After the diagnosis of paracoccidioidomycosis was confirmed, the TB treatment was discontinued. Due to the extensive pulmonary lesions and his HTLV-1 co-infection, he was started on treatment with amphotericin B, to be followed by itraconazole.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was chronic (adult) paracoccidioidomycosis. This was established by direct visualization of the characteristic yeast forms of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis on a KOH preparation of the patient's sputum, which was subsequently confirmed by fungal culture. The diagnosis was consistent with the patient's epidemiological risk factors (a male farmer from the Peruvian Amazon), chronic pulmonary symptoms with significant weight loss, and failure to respond to empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy.
